The article is a bit off, the bridge is not a "Cable Stayed" bridge, it is a post tensioned truss bridge. The vertical column and "cables" are aesthetic elements.

That is not to say that an engineering design flaw wasn't the cause (or at least a large factor) of the collapse.

Why the bridge failed

My understanding of the situation is that the the bridge was manufactured nearby (a bridge building method called ABC (Accelerated Bridge Construction)) and the main span was maneuvered into place using 4 SPMTs (Self Propelled Modular Transporter), 2 at each end. Due to obstructions in the road, one of the SPMTs needed to be moved further towards the center of the bridge. This meant that a larger section of the span was cantilevered over the end. This resulted in too much tension in one of the tensioning rods in the bridge trusses, causing it to stretch (it was loaded past its elastic limit). The stretched tension rod was now much weaker than it should be. When they lowered the span onto the supports, this tension rod was noticeably loose. So, they decided to tighten it (probably should have pondered why it was loose at this point). The rod was also easier to tighten than it should have been (another clue that it was failing). Rather than stop and get something in to hold up the bridge, they continued to tighten it. Eventually, this resulted in the tension rod failing under tension. You can see this in photos of the scene where the failed tension rod is shown pulled a couple of meters out of the truss (this can happen if it snaps under tension) Without the tension rod, the truss could not support the weight of the bridge and it failed catastrophically.

The design flaw

The primary design flaw here is that each of the tension rods was a single point of failure. There was no redundancy in the bridge at all. Which is mind boggling. Most bridges are built with several layers of redundancy, so that a lot of things would need to go badly wrong for it to fail. This bridge was guaranteed to collapse in the event of a single tension rod failure.

Mississippi Sheiks - Sitting on Top of the World (1930)

The title line of "Sitting on Top of the World" is similar to a well-known popular song of the 1920s, "I'm Sitting on Top of the World", written by Ray Henderson, Sam Lewis and Joe Young (popularised by Al Jolson in 1926). However the two songs are distinct, both musically and lyrically. Similarities have also been noted that "Sitting on Top of the World" was derived from an earlier song by Leroy Carr and Scrapper Blackwell, "You Got To Reap What You Sow" (1929). Tampa Red used the same melody in his version from the same year.

In May 1930, Charlie Patton recorded a version of the song (with altered lyrics) called “Some Summer Day” During the next few years renditions of "Sitting on Top of the World" were recorded by a number of artists: the Two Poor Boys, Doc Watson, Big Bill Broonzy, Sam Collins, Milton Brown and His Musical Brownies, and Bob Wills & His Texas Playboys. After Milton Brown recorded it for Bluebird Records the song became a staple in the repertoire of western swing bands.
